newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sees "great possibility" in IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sees "great possibility" in IRA truce.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday hailed the IRA's decision to resume a ceasefire in Northern Ireland and said the United States would work to nurture this "moment of great possibility."

"This declaration, which we expect to be implemented unequivocally and permanently, can open the door to inclusive negotations to achieve a just and lasting settlement," Clinton said in a statement issued by the White House.

The Irish Republican Army on Saturday announced a new truce in its 28-year war against British rule in Northern Ireland. It was to take effect at midday on Sunday and allow its Sinn Fein spokesmen a seat at peace talks.

Clinton, who has been more directly involved than any other U.S. president in trying to end the violence in Northern Ireland, publicly and privately has been pressing the IRA to reinstate a 17-month ceasefire it ended in February 1996.

"This is a moment of great possibility," Clinton said. "As Northern Ireland's political leaders begin to shape their future, I urge them to do so on the basis of the principles of fairness and compromise that underpin all democratic systems."
Declaration of a ceasefire paves the way for Sinn Fein to enter full-scale Northern Ireland negotiations that Britain and Ireland say must get under way by mid-September.
"The United States will work closely with the two governments and the political parties to build on this historic opportunity," Clinton said.
"On the basis of this ceasefire, implemented unequivocally, my administration will work with Sinn Fein as with the other political parties," he said.
"The United States will strongly support those who take the risks of principled compromise as they seek a peaceful and prosperous future for themselves and their children," he added.
Former U.S. Sen. George Mitchell chairs the formal peace talks, which have been bogged down for more than a year amid bitter acrimony between Protestant and Catholic parties.
The absence of Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, has undermined chances for real progress in resolving what have come to be known by the Irish as "the troubles."
Since coming to office in 1993, Clinton has put Northern Ireland high on his diplomatic agenda and in December 1995 became the first American president to visit the troubled province.

Clinton strained the traditionally close relations between London and Washington when he ignored British protests and granted Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams a visa to visit the United States in 1995 and invited him to the White House for a St. Patrick's Day reception.
Adams was last at the White House in February, 1996, just days before the IRA ended its last ceasefire with a massive bomb blast in London.
